questions.stem: Mrs Rao, 33, is on the birth suite with a primary PPH of 1,500 mL. Her fundus stays soft despite fundal massage and oxytocin. She has had analgesia and has agreed to bimanual compression. The examiner asks you to show it on the model. Where do you place your hands?
options: Fist in the posterior fornix; abdominal hand pressing the fundus down towards the pelvis
Fist inside the uterine cavity; abdominal hand pressing firmly over the suprapubic region
Fist in the anterior fornix; abdominal hand behind the uterus, pressing it forwards
Two fingers on the cervix; abdominal hand rubbing the fundus in firm circular movements
questions.why: In bimanual compression a closed fist goes in the anterior vaginal fornix and the abdominal hand cups the back of the uterus. The uterine body is squeezed between the two hands. Keep it up until the bleeding is controlled or she is in theatre.
notes: A fist in the posterior fornix does not give a firm surface to squeeze the uterine body against, and pushing the fundus down only moves the uterus without compressing it.
Putting a hand inside the uterine cavity is manual exploration or removal under anaesthesia, not bimanual compression, and suprapubic pressure does not compress the uterine body.
Fingers on the cervix with fundal rubbing is just fundal massage, which has already failed; it does not compress the uterus between two hands.

questions.stem: Mrs Rao, 33, gave birth vaginally 30 minutes ago and has a primary PPH of 1,500 mL from an atonic uterus. She is having oxytocin and second-line uterotonics. HR 124, BP 92/56. She has no bleeding disorder and takes no anticoagulants. How should tranexamic acid be used for her?
options: 1 g IV over 10 minutes now, with a second 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 minutes
1 g orally now, then repeated every 8 hours for 24 hours
1 g IV, but only once results show a fibrinogen below 2 g/L
1 g IV, but only if bleeding continues more than 3 hours after the birth
questions.why: Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes as soon as possible in PPH, within 3 hours of birth, whatever the cause. Give a second 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours. The benefit falls the longer it is delayed.
notes: Oral tranexamic acid is too slow and unreliable for a woman bleeding heavily in shock; it is given IV in PPH.
Tranexamic acid is given early whatever the cause, without waiting for coagulation results; low fibrinogen needs replacement with fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate.
Benefit is greatest when given early, and there is no benefit (and possible harm) when it is started more than 3 hours after birth.

questions.stem: Mrs Rao, 33, has a soft, boggy fundus above the umbilicus 25 minutes after the birth of a 4.3 kg baby, and blood and clots keep coming through the cervix. Her clotting is normal. What is the main way the uterus normally stops bleeding from the placental bed after birth?
options: Platelet plugs and fibrin at the placental bed seal the spiral arteries without help
Sympathetic vasoconstriction of the uterine arteries reduces blood flow to the uterus
Prostaglandins from the decidua directly constrict the spiral arteries without help
Contracting, interlacing myometrial fibres kink and compress the spiral arteries
questions.why: Interlacing myometrial fibres contract and retract around the spiral arteries that run through them, squeezing the vessels shut (the 'living ligatures'). In atony this mechanical squeeze is lost, so the placental bed bleeds heavily even when clotting is normal.
notes: Clotting helps but cannot seal open spiral arteries carrying about 500 to 700 mL/min at term on its own, so atony bleeds even with normal coagulation.
The uterine circulation is near maximally dilated at term and responds little to sympathetic tone; vasoconstriction is not the main way bleeding stops.
Prostaglandins act mainly by making the myometrium contract (as carboprost does), not by directly constricting the spiral arteries on their own.

questions.stem: Mrs Rao, 33, is still bleeding from an atonic uterus after 1,500 mL of loss. The registrar says that if the bleeding goes on after the retained tissue is removed, uterine artery embolisation or ligation may be needed. The uterine artery is a branch of which vessel?
options: Posterior division of the internal iliac artery
Anterior division of the internal iliac artery
External iliac artery, just above the inguinal ligament
Abdominal aorta, just below the renal arteries
questions.why: The uterine artery comes off the anterior division of the internal iliac artery. It runs medially in the base of the broad ligament and crosses above the ureter ('water under the bridge') near the cervix, which is why the ureter is at risk during ligation.
notes: The posterior division gives the iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal arteries, which supply the body wall and buttock, not the pelvic organs.
The external iliac artery supplies the lower limb and gives the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries, not the uterine artery.
The vessel that arises from the aorta below the renal arteries is the ovarian artery, which joins up with the uterine artery but is a separate vessel.
